name: Slicks of a shape seen once
brief:
A satellite image of a shipping lane marks oil as `#` and clear water as `.`, given as `grid`, a list of equal-length strings. A slick is a group of `#` cells joined through shared sides. Two slicks have the same shape when one can be slid onto the other, without turning or flipping it. Return how many slicks have a shape that no other slick shares.

Write `lone_shapes(grid)`.

Example. In `['#.#', '#.#', '...', '##.']` the two upright pairs have the same shape and the flat pair has its own. So the answer is 1.
constraints: $O(\text{rows} \times \text{cols})$ time is the target, using a hashable description of each shape.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Fill each slick from its first cell in reading order, and record every cell as an offset from that first cell. A `frozenset` of offsets describes the shape; count how often each one occurs.

examples.note: The two upright pairs match; the flat pair is the only one of its shape.
Both slicks have three cells, but one cannot be slid onto the other, so both count.

tests.call: lone_shapes([''.join('#' if (i % 3 < 2 and j % 3 < 2) or (i, j) == (0, 2) else '.' for j in range(300)) for i in range(300)])

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Offsets from a slick's first cell in reading order are the same for every slid copy, so they name the shape.
A string of search moves without a mark for each step back can give two different shapes the same name.
Each cell is visited once and each shape is hashed once, so the work is $O(\text{rows} \times \text{cols})$.

planted.slip: Comparing slicks by their number of cells treats different shapes of the same size as one.
Naming a shape by its search moves, with no mark for stepping back, gives two different shapes one name.
Counting distinct shapes answers a different question: a shape seen twice still counts once.
